A close reading for the week

“a wild rose-bush”

The Scarlet Letter · Chapter 1

The novel opens at a prison door in Puritan Boston, all iron, oak and weather-stains, with one wild rose-bush flowering at the threshold. Before any character appears, Hawthorne has set out the book’s argument in a doorway.

The rust on the ponderous iron-work of its oaken door looked more antique than anything else in the New World.1 Like all that pertains to crime, it seemed never to have known a youthful era. Before this ugly edifice, and between it and the wheel-track of the street, was a grass-plot, much overgrown with burdock, pigweed, apple-peru, and such unsightly vegetation, which evidently found something congenial in the soil that had so early borne the black flower of civilized society, a prison.2

  1. 1

    Old before its time

    The “New World” is barely a generation old, and already its most antique object is a prison door. The next sentence states the principle: whatever pertains to crime “seemed never to have known a youthful era”. Utopian settlement, Hawthorne implies, ages instantly at the point where it must punish; the chapter has already noted that the founders’ first allotments were a cemetery and a prison.

  2. 2

    The black flower

    The prison is “the black flower of civilized society”, an oxymoron that keeps growing. Flowers bloom from congenial soil; so, the sentence says, do prisons, and the weeds around this one (burdock, pigweed, apple-peru, named like a botanist’s list) find the soil “congenial” too. Civilisation builds its prison and also cultivates it. The metaphor sets up the rose as the counter-flower before the rose appears.
